name: V-Y advancement / vermilion advancement
lead: Vermilion advancement is a group of surgical techniques that move or advance the pink lip tissue, the vermilion, to rebuild or enlarge it. In the literature it is mostly a reconstructive method, for example after tumour removal from the lip, while in cosmetic surgery it is discussed as a way to increase pink lip show and to shape the lip border.[1][2][3] For someone who wants fuller, better-defined lips without an injectable or implant, advancing the person's own lip tissue is one of the surgical routes described.

A 1996 review of cosmetic lip surgery opens by noting that full, well-defined lips are associated with youth, health and attractiveness and that thin, flat lips imply fragility, and then presents aesthetic guidelines on Cupid's bow, upper lip length and projection.[1] Reconstructive reports describe modified Goldstein-type bilateral vermilion flaps after Mohs surgery for lip squamous cell carcinoma[2] and a vermilion advancement flap with a facial artery musculomucosal flap after buccal mucosa tumour resection.[3]
Little published research covers vermilion advancement as a purely cosmetic operation, and the V-Y advancement flap is used across surgery for many other body sites.

chain: Pink lip tissue is advanced toward the lip border
More vermilion shows, or a defect is rebuilt
angle.text: Advancing lip mucosa changes how much pink lip is visible and how defined the lip border looks. Surgeons use it mainly to rebuild the lip after cancer surgery, and cosmetic surgeons describe related approaches for people who want more lip show.

infobox: Lip lift, V-Y flap, Abbe flap, Karapandzic flap[4]
V-Y lip augmentation, an intraoral incision with no external scar [17]

paras: Advancement flaps slide adjacent mucosa or skin into a defect or toward a desired border. In lip reconstruction after tumour removal, authors describe bilateral flaps that expand tissue to cover vermilion defects.[2] Other reports pair vermilion advancement with additional flaps for defects of the oral commissure.[3][5][6]

A V-Y advancement is a flap design in which a V-shaped incision is moved forward and closed in a Y pattern, lengthening or shifting tissue; surgeons use the pattern at many sites, and several trials in the research literature concern pilonidal disease, pressure sores and anal fissures rather than the lip.[7][8]

The vermilion is the red-pink part of the lip, bounded by the vermilion border where it meets paler facial skin. Wikipedia explains that it looks red because the skin is thin and sits over many capillaries; unlike oral mucosa it has a cornified outer layer and no salivary glands, and unlike ordinary skin it lacks hair follicles and sweat glands.[4] The pattern of the border defines the philtrum, the two vertical lines forming the bow of the central upper lip; the commissures where upper and lower lips meet; and the lateral upper lip.[4]

Underneath lies the orbicularis oris, a circular muscle that closes the mouth and keeps food and fluids in (oral competence).[4] The upper lip is supplied with sensation by the infraorbital nerve and the lower lip by the mental nerve, while blood comes mainly from branches of the facial artery, which is why flaps are planned around these supplies.[4] A 2018 review notes that the lip has three layers, mucosa, muscle and skin, and that which layers a defect involves guides the choice of repair.[9]

Wikipedia's article on lip reconstruction says reconstruction follows trauma or cancer excision, since the lips are a common site of oral cancer, and that it aims to preserve sensation, oral competence, a continuous vermilion border and an acceptable appearance.[4] A 2018 review of lip reconstruction after Mohs surgery describes an algorithm based on defect location, tissue involvement and severity, and notes the three anatomical layers of the lip: mucosa, muscle and skin.[9]

For superficial lower-lip defects limited to the vermilion, the Wikipedia article lists A-T closure or single or double advancement among the options.[4] Larger full-thickness defects use other flaps: the Abbe flap for roughly one-third to two-thirds of the lip, taking tissue from the opposite lip and dividing the pedicle after 10 to 14 days; the Karapandzic flap, which preserves nerve and blood supply but can narrow the mouth opening; and the Gillies fan flap.[4] Reported complications of lip reconstruction include a poor cosmetic result, loss of oral competence, small mouth size, reduced sensation and recurrence of disease.[4]

Five goals are listed for lip reconstruction: preserve sensation, maintain oral competence, keep the vermilion border continuous, leave enough mouth opening to avoid a very small mouth (microstoma), and give the lip an acceptable appearance.[4] Superficial defects of the skin and vermilion that leave muscle and nerves intact are handled differently from full-thickness defects. For the central upper lip, a straight-line closure may pull the vermilion border upward as it heals, while advancement flaps that bring in tissue from one or both sides suit defects that span the full height of the lip.[4] For the lateral lip, options include straight closure, an A-T closure that hides the scar along the philtrum or border, single advancement along the vermilion border, and rotation flaps from the cheek.[4]

For the lower lip, anatomic requirements are described as less limiting; key aims are keeping the vermilion border undistorted, hiding incisions in the horizontal chin crease and not distorting the commissure.[4] Small defects, up to about a quarter of the upper lip or a third of the lower lip, can be closed directly in three layers of mucosa, muscle and skin, which the article says gives the best outcome.[4]

sections.h: V-Y lip augmentation and lip lifts
paras: Wikipedia's lip lift article describes V-Y lip augmentation, also called V-Y lip advancement, as an operation in which an incision inside the mouth advances mucosa and vermilion outward. It leaves no exposed external scar, but is described as potentially painful with a lengthy recovery, citing work by Aiache (1997) and Rohrich and colleagues (2000). [17] Internal scars may take two to four months to heal, and patients are advised to rest for at least a week. [17]

Lip lifts, by contrast, remove skin and reposition it. The direct or gull-wing lift removes skin at or above the white roll to raise the vermilion, and the subnasal bullhorn lift removes an ellipse under the nose so that more upper-lip vermilion shows. [17] Lip lifts were developed in the 1980s after collagen fillers proved limited for lasting correction, and improved non-surgical fillers are said to have reduced demand. [17]

A study by Jacono and Quatela (2004) reported statistically significant gains in upper vermilion height and surface area with V-Y augmentation, and a 2014 systematic review by San Miguel Moragas and colleagues found philtrum length decreased with indirect lip lifts but not with V-Y augmentation. [17] The article notes that surgeons report high patient satisfaction but that no single technique is the standard. [17]

Reported complications of lip lifts and related operations include numbness, stiffness, pain, paresthesia, lip distortion or lengthening, smile deformation, speech difficulty and visible or hypertrophic scarring. [17]

sections.h: The vermilion border and why alignment matters
paras: The vermilion border is the usually sharp line between lip and facial skin, where the epidermis shifts from heavily keratinised outer skin to less keratinised lip tissue; it has no sebaceous glands, sweat glands or hair. [18] The Cupid's bow is formed by two adjacent elevations of the border along the upper lip, and the border is a focal point for cosmetics such as lipstick. [18] Sun exposure can blur its edge, and lip balm and sunscreen can help protect it. [18] Wikipedia notes that even 1 mm of misalignment when the border is repaired after surgery such as vermilionectomy can be noticeable, which is why surgeons planning advancement flaps work to keep the border continuous. [18]

The 1996 Facial Plastic Surgery review sets out aesthetic guidelines for Cupid's bow shape, the relative length of the upper lip and lip projection or bulk, the characteristics it identifies as responsible for how lips are perceived.[1]

Alongside surgery, Wikipedia's lip augmentation article describes injectable fillers, fat transfer and implants as other ways people change lip volume, and notes that overfilling can look unnatural.[10] Vermilion advancement is distinct from these because it repositions the person's own tissue.

Wikipedia's lip augmentation article describes a spectrum of approaches to changing lip appearance: injectable fillers of different materials and durations, fat transfer, implants such as ePTFE strips, and surgical flap augmentation, in which small pieces of nearby skin or inner-mouth tissue are moved into the lip, adding little volume and only slight protrusion.[10] Temporary measures include lip plumpers containing irritants such as capsaicin and suction devices.[10] Common effects of filler procedures include redness, swelling, itching and bruising for days to a week, and overfilling can produce an exaggerated look.[10]

Vermilion advancement, by contrast, uses the person's own mucosa and does not introduce foreign material. In the cosmetic setting, people who discuss it describe it as a way to show more pink lip or define the border; the published literature on cosmetic indications is thin, and most detailed descriptions are from reconstruction after cancer or injury.[1][2][3]

sections.h: The V-Y flap pattern in other surgery
paras: V-Y advancement is a general surgical principle used on many parts of the body, which is why the term appears widely in the literature. Reviews describe V-Y tendon advancement for chronic Achilles tendon ruptures,[12][13] V-Y flaps for recalcitrant pilonidal disease,[14] and V-Y flaps for sacral pressure sores and for chronic anal fissures.[8][15] The Keystone flap uses V-Y advancement of each end of an islanded flap to close defects after skin cancer removal.[16] A prospective randomised trial compared the V-Y advancement flap with primary suture in pilonidal disease.[7]

Evidence is limited to surgical case reports and reconstruction series; published reports of vermilion advancement are mainly case-level, and controlled trials in cosmetic use have not been located.[2][3][5][6]  A 2018 report describes bilateral tissue-expanding vermilion myocutaneous flaps (a Goldstein technique modified by Sawada) for lower-lip repair after Mohs surgery for squamous cell carcinoma, a cancer that is the most common malignancy of the lower lip and for which Mohs surgery is described as the treatment of choice with the lowest recurrence rates.[2]

A 2017 case report describes a 62-year-old woman with carcinoma in situ of the buccal mucosa whose resection included the labial angle and who was reconstructed in one stage with a facial artery musculomucosal flap and a vermilion advancement flap, an approach used when more than one-third of the lip is involved.[3]

A 2018 study defined the standard morphology of the oral commissure in 50 normal Japanese volunteers and then evaluated ten patients with full-thickness cheek defects involving the commissure after free flap reconstruction.[5] A 2014 report describes lower lip repair with double opposing rectangular rotation flaps.[6] A 1996 review set out aesthetic principles for cosmetic lip surgery.[1] A registered trial compares techniques in unilateral cleft lip repair, a related but distinct area; it enrolled 68 people and started in 2018.[11]

card.summary: Flap surgery that moves pink lip tissue; mostly reconstructive, with little cosmetic research.
card.note: Cosmetic use has little published evidence.

quick.overview:
Vermilion advancement slides lip tissue to rebuild or enlarge the pink lip. Most reports concern reconstruction after cancer surgery.
Cosmetic use is thinly documented.
quick.mechanism: Flaps of lip tissue are advanced toward the lip border to restore or increase vermilion.
quick.risks: Surgical scarring and asymmetry are general concerns; cosmetic-specific data have not been published.
